paragraphs: Nowadays, some parents teach their teenage children at home instead of sending them to school. A lot of people talk about it and it is a very interesting topic. In this essay I will write about home education.

Home education has a lot of advantages. Firstly, students can learn in their own speed. Secondly, they can get up later. Thirdly, they do not have to travel to school. Finally, they can learn about things they like.

On the other hand, home education also has disadvantages. The biggest problem is that students do not meet people in their age every day. At school, students make friends, go on trips and learn how to work in a group, for example when they prepare a project with their classmates. At home it is much more difficult. Moreover, parents must to spend a lot of time on teaching, so one of them often cannot work. If a student will have problems with maths or physics, the parents may not be able to help. Of course, it depends from the family.

To sum up, some parents teach their teenage children at home instead of sending them to school. In my opinion, home education has advantages and disadvantages and every family should decide for itself.

paragraphs: For most teenagers, school is where learning happens. However, some parents choose to educate their children at home instead of sending them to secondary school. This approach offers real benefits, but it also comes with drawbacks that families should weigh carefully.

The greatest advantage is flexibility. Without a fixed timetable, students can spend more time on subjects they find difficult and move quickly through those they have already mastered. A teenager who struggles with chemistry, for instance, can devote a whole week to it instead of falling further behind. Furthermore, learning can be shaped around individual interests. A student passionate about programming or music can pursue that interest seriously, which is rarely possible alongside a seven-hour school day.

On the other hand, home education can be isolating. School is not only about lessons; it is also where teenagers make friends, learn to cooperate and deal with conflict. Although home-educated students can join clubs or sports teams, they spend far less time with people of their own age. Another drawback is the pressure on parents. Teaching several subjects at an advanced level requires knowledge and time, which often means one parent has to give up work.

All things considered, home education can work well for highly motivated teenagers whose parents have the time and skills to support them. For most students, however, the social side of school is too valuable to lose, so in my view it should remain the exception rather than the rule.

paragraphs: A first job used to mean a desk in an office. Today, however, some companies hire graduates who will never set foot in an office at all. Working entirely from home can be a real opportunity for someone starting their career, yet it also carries risks that are easy to underestimate.

The most obvious advantage is the time and money saved on commuting. Instead of spending an hour on a crowded bus, a young employee can use that hour to sleep, exercise or study. Another major benefit is that there is no need to move to an expensive city. A graduate from a small town can work for a company in Warsaw without paying high rent, which makes a first salary go much further.

However, for a beginner the drawbacks may be even more significant. Much of what young people learn at work comes from watching experienced colleagues and asking quick questions, which is far harder through a screen. A junior programmer, for example, may wait hours for an answer that someone at the next desk could give in a minute. Furthermore, newcomers who meet their managers only online find it harder to build relationships and get noticed.

On balance, I believe that working only from home is not the best start for most young people. A hybrid arrangement, with at least a few days a week in the office, would let them keep some of these benefits while still learning from others.

paragraphs: Not so long ago, seeing a doctor meant taking time off school or work and spending an hour in a crowded waiting room. Now many patients can describe their symptoms over the phone or during a video call. Such remote consultations have obvious advantages, but they also have limitations.

The main benefit is convenience. A short call takes minutes, so patients do not have to travel or wait, which matters especially for people living in villages far from the nearest clinic. Remote advice is also well suited to simple matters, such as getting a repeat prescription or discussing test results. What is more, staying at home protects others. A patient with a high temperature does not have to sit among elderly people and risk passing on an infection.

Nevertheless, a doctor who cannot physically examine the patient may miss important signs. Listening to someone's chest or pressing on a painful stomach is impossible from a distance, so a serious illness could be mistaken for a minor one. Moreover, remote consultations are not equally easy for everyone. Many older patients find video calls confusing, and people with hearing problems may struggle with a poor connection. For them, a visit in person remains the safer option.

All in all, remote consultations are a useful addition to traditional appointments, but they cannot replace them. In my view, they work best for follow-up questions and minor problems, while anything that requires a physical examination should still be handled face to face.

paragraphs: Space missions cost enormous sums, so it is no wonder that some people would rather see this money spent on hospitals or schools. However, I am convinced that cutting space research would be a mistake, both because it improves life on Earth and because the case for cutting it is weaker than it first appears.

Much of modern life depends on work done in space. Weather satellites allow forecasters to warn people about storms and floods days in advance, which saves lives and protects crops. Satellite navigation, which guides ambulances and delivery drivers alike, would not exist without decades of space research. What is more, images taken from orbit help scientists track melting glaciers and forest fires, which is vital for understanding climate change.

Admittedly, the money could be used to tackle pressing problems such as poverty or long hospital waiting lists. Yet this argument assumes that governments must choose one or the other. In reality, space agencies receive only a small share of public spending, so cutting their budgets would hardly solve any major problem. Moreover, space programmes create jobs for engineers and can inspire young people to study science, which benefits the economy in the long run.

For all these reasons, I strongly believe that governments should keep investing in space exploration. Rather than cutting these budgets, they should explain how much everyday life depends on satellites. Space research is not an expensive luxury but an investment whose benefits are felt on Earth.

paragraphs: Traffic jams, noise and polluted air have become part of everyday life in many city centres. One radical solution is to close them to private cars altogether. In my opinion, such a ban would make city centres far better places to live, but only if the authorities prepare for it carefully.

The most noticeable change would be cleaner and quieter streets. With fewer exhaust fumes, people with asthma could breathe more easily, and residents could sleep with the windows open. Moreover, space now used for parking could be turned into wider pavements, cycle lanes and small parks, where neighbours could meet and children could play safely. Admittedly, some residents, especially older people, might find it harder to get around at first, which is why good preparation is essential.

First and foremost, the city would need to improve public transport before the ban comes into force. Trams and buses should run more frequently, including late in the evening, and tickets should be cheap enough to compete with driving. Secondly, there should be exceptions for people who genuinely depend on a car, such as disabled drivers. Finally, park-and-ride car parks on the outskirts would let commuters switch to the tram.

To conclude, closing city centres to cars is not about punishing drivers but about giving streets back to people. If the change is introduced gradually and residents are offered real alternatives, I am sure most of them will soon wonder how they ever put up with the traffic.

annotations.quote: such as disabled drivers
annotations.note_pl: Kolejne działanie z przykładem. Trzy konkretne propozycje (komunikacja, wyjątki, parkingi) to realizacja wieloaspektowa, więc 2 pkt.

annotations.quote: is not about punishing drivers but about giving streets back to people
annotations.note_pl: Konstrukcja not about… but about… zbiera myśl całego tekstu w jedno zdanie.

annotations.quote: I am sure most of them will soon wonder how they ever put up with the traffic
annotations.note_pl: Zakończenie zgodne z tezą, ale innymi słowami i z przewidywaniem, które wynika z akapitów. Za zakończenie 2 pkt.

models.comment_pl: Szacunek: zgodność z poleceniem 5/5 (treść 10/10, forma 4/4), spójność 2/2, zakres 3/3, poprawność 3/3, razem 13/13. Tak wygląda rozprawka z opinią, w której jeden element to rozwiązanie problemu. Zauważ, że trudność dla mieszkańców pojawia się w akapicie 2, ale tylko jako most do propozycji, więc nie przeczy tezie. Element typu „zaproponuj” w rozprawce to rzadkość: w latach 2023–2026 był tylko w liście (2025), a wszystkie rozprawki były „za i przeciw”. Ten temat to trening na wypadek rozprawki z opinią, którą informator dopuszcza.
